newsitem.title: JAPAN: TIFFE Euroyen ends Tokyo up on swap-related buying.
newsitem.headline: TIFFE Euroyen ends Tokyo up on swap-related buying.

text.p: The key June three-month Euroyen deposit rate contract ended firmer in Tokyo on Tuesday, in reaction to purchases by banks to hedge against their payments of fixed interest rates in the swap market, traders said.
The June was also supported by a cabinet minister's remark urging the central bank to maintain its easy credit stance, and by weak machinery orders data for September, traders said.
"It is desirable for the BOJ to maintain its easy credit policy for the time being," Economic Planning Agency (EPA) Minister Taro Aso told a news conference.
Bids on the June emerged after a few city banks paid fixed interest rates and received floating rates, traders said.

Some said these swap transactions may be related to the large issue volume for the key three month certificates of deposit (CDs). Approximately 1.1 trillion yen worth of the key CDs was traded at 0.52 percent.
The banks appeared to have shifted a part of their fund raising demand from the call market to the CDs, traders said.

EPA's Aso also said economic indicators that have been announced recently show the economy is recovering gradually, although it was too early to say whether the driving force has completely shifted to private demand from public demand.

In the afternoon, the June contract rose to a high of 99.13 right after data was released showing a sharp 10.2 percent month-on-month drop in private machinery orders for September. However, the June soon gave up a part of its gains as the EPA also gave its forecast for a steep 19.3 percent rise in orders for October-December against the previous quarter, they said. It recovered ground by the close on city banks' buying.

The visiting chairman of the London International Financial Futures and Options Exchange (LIFFE), Jack Wigglesworth, said on Tuesday that the exchange will consider measures to increase the popularity of three-month Euroyen futures in London, but added that light turnover on LIFFE was inevitable.

"One should never expect the volume of derivatives products...outside the time zone of the underlying market to be as great as the volume of turnover...in the home market," he said. Wigglesworth was speaking at a luncheon in Tokyo.
